papers.title_in_file: LEARNING THE COMPLEXITY OF WEAKLY NOISY QUANTUM STATES
papers.version_note: The text layer holds the paper twice (arXiv v4 of 21 May 2025, the ICLR 2025 conference version, 30 pages, then the same text appended). The first copy was read in full; the second was not needed. The file name carries the 2023 arXiv title (Complexity analysis of weakly noisy quantum states via quantum machine learning); the text is the later retitled version of the same arXiv id 2303.17813.
papers.what_it_is: A conference paper that gives a classical-shadow-based learning algorithm that predicts a limited-structure circuit complexity of weakly noisy quantum states, with stated sample and running-time bounds and small simulations.

existing.note: The theorem on efficiency holds for noisy depth of order log n, for the structured complexity prediction task (which has an indeterminate case), and for an ideal learner device. The sample lower bound theorem is proved for a different task (Task 2 in Appendix J: telling apart the outputs of two noisy circuits of different depth), not for the prediction task, and it grows only linearly in the noisy depth. The body calls the algorithm nearly optimal in the depth; only the abstract says optimal. The upper bound on samples is stated without a derivation in the paper.
existing.value: The paper states that, for poly(n) copies of a weakly noisy state of depth R = O(log n) and a particular architecture A, a learning algorithm of poly(n, R, 1/ε) quantum and classical cost solves the structured complexity prediction problem SCP(A, ε), and that the sample complexity lower bound may grow linearly with the circuit layer, so that the algorithm is nearly optimal in the circuit depth; the abstract calls the algorithm optimal in sample complexity with polynomial classical processing time.

quotes: Given poly(n) copies of an n-qubit unknown weakly noisy state ρun that is generated by a noisy quantum device with depth R ̃ = O(log n) (Def. 2)
and a particular architecture A, there exists a poly(n, R ̃, 1/ε) quantum and classical cost learning algorithm which can efficiently solve the SCP(A, ε) problem.
This implies the sample complexity lower bound may linearly growth with the increasing of the circuit layer R ̃, and our learning algorithm is nearly-optimal in terms of the circuit depth
Our algorithm is proved to be optimal in terms of sample complexity accompanied with polynomial classical processing time.
existing.certainty_reason: Theorem 2 is proved only as an outline in Sections 5.1 and 5.2; the sample bounds do not match in n (see the Theorem 3 entry).
existing.reader_inference: The upper sample bound (order n squared L R log n log(1/δ) over ε to the fourth) and the lower bound (order one over n times (1 + 2cpR)(1 - δ) squared) share only the linear dependence on depth. With constant δ the quoted lower bound is below one sample for every n, if 2n means two times n (the text layer cannot show whether it means 2 to the n). So the word optimal rests on the depth dependence only; the reader did not find a tight bound in n.

existing.note: The paper's main-text comparison uses only two noisy depths (2 and 10), one lattice size (3 × 4), 10 repetitions per point and lower bounds from Lemma 2 (the estimate of a lower bound, not of the complexity). The claim is hedged in the paper as 'may not grow'. Appendix L repeats the comparison in one dimension for sizes 6, 8 and 10.
existing.value: The authors report that, in simulation of the time dynamics of a transverse-field Ising model on a two-dimensional grid, with system size 3 × 4 and each gate under a local depolarizing channel with strength p = 10−3, the estimated lower bounds were above 4L for the noisy depth 2 state and above 2L for the noisy depth 10 state, and they state that the lower bound of weakly noisy states may not grow with the circuit depth and that shallower circuit weakly noisy states possess a higher lower bound.
quotes: C0li.m12,A5 (ρTI(R ̃ = 10, p)) > 2L and C0li.m12,A5 (ρTI(R ̃ = 2, p)) > 4L (according to Lemma 2)
This result highlights weakly noisy quantum state complexity lower bound may not grow with the circuit depth, which is dramatically different to that of pure states.
where a shallower circuit depth weakly noisy states possess higher state complexity lower bound.
where the system size is 3 × 4, angle rotations −2Jδt = −π/2, hδt ∈ {π/8, π/4, π/2, 3π/4, π} and each quantum gate is affected by a local depolarizing channel Ei with strength p = 10−3.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulated study.
existing.reader_inference: A lower bound that is smaller at larger depth does not by itself show that the complexity itself is smaller; the paper reports only the Lemma 2 side, by design (its footnote 7).

existing.note: The paper's definition of weakly noisy states names a gate-independent Pauli channel (the stored value says a general channel). Theorem 2 needs noisy depth of order log n (the stored value says shallow), and the learner is on an ideal device. The size of the noise is p below order 1/n.
existing.value: The paper restricts attention to weakly noisy states: noisy depth at most poly log n and noise strength of order 1/n; the noise is a gate-independent, time-invariant channel, and its definition of a weakly noisy state models the noise as a gate-independent Pauli noise channel with error rate p; its efficiency theorem further needs depth of order log n, and the learning task runs on an ideal quantum device.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing prior work, that the lower bound on pure-state complexity grows linearly with system size, and that extending this to noisy circuit environments remains an open challenge and that characterizing the noisy state complexity is still an open problem.
quotes: The lower bound on quantum pure state complexity has been shown to grow linearly with system size (Haferkamp et al., 2022). However, extending this result to noisy circuit environments, which better reflect real quantum devices, remains an open challenge.
and how to characterize the noisy quantum state complexity is still an open problem.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to Haferkamp et al. (2022) and a statement about the literature.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing two prior works, that noisy states prepared by Ω(log n)-depth noisy circuits are classically simulable in both mean value computation and random circuit sampling, with a constant level of noise in each gate, and that increasing the depth of the noisy circuit reduces the quantum state complexity.
quotes: resulting in noisy states prepared by Ω(log n)-depth noisy circuits is classically simulable in both mean value computation and random circuit sampling problems
increasing the depth of the noisy circuit reduces the quantum state complexity.
assertions.certainty_reason: Cited results; the second sentence is the authors' reading of them.

assertions.value: The paper adopts, from earlier work, a definition: a pure state has ε-strong state complexity at most c if and only if the maximal bias over measurement operators built from at most c two-qubit gates reaches the quoted threshold, denoted Cε(|ψ⟩) ≤ c.
quotes: Definition 1 (Approximate State Complexity (Branda ̃o et al., 2021)) Given an integer c and ε ∈ (0, 1), we say a pure quantum state |ψ⟩ has ε-strong state complexity at most c if and only if ξQS(c, |ψ⟩) ≥ 1 − 2n − ε, (3) which is denoted as Cε(|ψ⟩) ≤ c.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition attributed to Brandão et al. (2021).
assertions.reader_inference: The threshold is printed in the text layer as '1 − 2n − ε' (a power of two with the sign lost); the reader takes it to mean one minus two to the power minus n, minus ε, as the preceding text says the bias degenerates to that value.

assertions.value: The paper defines the noisy state with noise strength p of depth R as the output of alternating noise channels and causal slices on the all-zero state, assuming a gate-independent Pauli noise channel with error rate p, and calls the states with depth at most poly log n and error rate p below order 1/n weakly noisy.
quotes: Definition 2 (Weakly Noisy Quantum State) We assume that the noise in the quantum device is modeled by a gate-independent Pauli noise channel E with error rate p. Let U be a causal slice, and let E ◦ U be the representation of a noisy gate.
We use the term "weakly noisy quantum states" to refer to noisy states ρp,R ̃ with R ̃ ≤ O(poly log n) and small error rate p such that p < O(n−1).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition (Definition 2).

assertions.value: The paper defines a weakly noisy state to have ε-LS complexity at most c if the maximal bias of measurement operators of the form U|0n⟩⟨0n|U† with U from the architecture class of depth ⌈c/L⌉ against the maximally mixed state reaches the quoted threshold, where L is the number of gates in each layer, and calls ε the LS error.
quotes: Definition 3 (Limited-Structured (LS) Complexity of Weakly Noisy State) Given an integer c and ε ∈ (0, 1), we say a weakly noisy state ρ has ε-LS complexity at most c if and only if max |Tr (Mc(ρ − In/2n))| Mc=U |0n⟩⟨0n|U † ≥ 1− 1 2n −ε (5) U ∈UA([c/L]) which is denoted as Cεlim,A(ρ) ≤ c.
The notation L represents the number of gates in each layer of U ∈ UA4, and ε is termed as the LS error.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition (Definition 3).

assertions.value: The authors state that the LS complexity provides an upper bound for the state complexity of the weakly noisy state, that is Cε(ρ) ≤ Cεlim,A(ρ) ≤ c.
quotes: It is interesting to note that the LS complexity provides an upper bound for Cε(ρun), that is, Cε(ρ) ≤ Cεlim,A(ρ) ≤ c.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement; Definition 1 is for pure states and the paper gives no separate proof of this sentence beyond Fact 1.

The paper then says Eq. 7 implies a state for which the overlap is high 'in the worst-case scenario over the choice of U1, ..., UR'. An average bound shows that some choice reaches the average, not that every weakly noisy state does. The reader did not find the step that closes this gap.

assertions.value: The paper defines the task SCP(A, ε): given an architecture A, a weakly noisy n-qubit state and an approximation error ε, design a learning algorithm QLn that runs on an ideal quantum device with polynomially many qubits in n, that returns True if an integer x < log n lies in UDI(ε) (completeness), False if log n ∈ LDI(ε) (soundness), and either answer arbitrarily if all integers in [0, log n] lie outside both intervals (indeterminate case).
quotes: design a learning algorithm QLn that runs on an ideal quantum device with polynomially many qubits in n
1. (Completeness) If there exists an integer x < log n such that x ∈ UDI(ε), then QLn returns True.
2. (Soundness) If log n ∈ LDI(ε), then QLn returns False.
3. (Indeterminate case) If all integers x ∈ [0, log n] lie in UDIc(ε) ∪ LDIc(ε), then QLn may return either True or False arbitrarily.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own task definition.

assertions.value: The paper defines the upper decision interval UDI(ε) as the integer interval [u, ∞) on which max LR(β) ≤ ε holds and the lower decision interval LDI(ε) as the integer interval [0, l] on which min LR(β) ≥ 2ε holds.
quotes: Definition 4 (Decision interval) UDI(ε) is defined as the integer interval [u, ∞) such that for any R ∈ UDI(ε), it holds that maxβ⃗ LR β⃗ ≤ ε.
Similarly, LDI(ε) is defined as the integer interval [0, l] such that for any R ∈ LDI(ε), we have minβ⃗ LR β⃗ ≥ 2ε.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition.

assertions.value: The paper defines the property DP(A, ε): a weakly noisy state has it if it can be distinguished from the maximally mixed state with bias at least the quoted threshold by an R-depth (R < log n) measurement U|0n⟩⟨0n|U† with U from the architecture class; the algorithm returns True (False) to indicate that the state does (does not) have it.
quotes: Definition 5 (Distinguishable Property, DP(A, ε)) We say an n-qubit weakly noisy quantum state ρun satisfies DP(A, ε) if ρun can be distinguished from In/2n with the bias at least 1 − 2−n − ε by using a R-depth (R < log n) QCA measurement MQCA = U |0n⟩⟨0n|U †, where U ∈ UA.
We note that the learning algorithm QLn returns True (respectively, False) to indicate that ρun does (does not) satisfy the DP(A, ε) property.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition.

assertions.value: The paper defines the metric LR(β) = Eρi∼q Tr M(β)(ρi − ρ) over the compact set Dβ, and assumes Dβ = [0, 1]N to keep the semi-definite property of M(β).
assertions.anchor: Section 4.1, Equation 11 and footnote 6, p.6, p.6

To keep the semi-definite property of M (β⃗), we generally assume the compact set Dβ = [0, 1]N .
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition and assumption.

assertions.value: The authors state that, because the architecture class of lower depth is strictly contained in that of higher depth (citing Haferkamp et al., 2022), the predicate P(R, ε) = BMaxS(...) is monotone in R ∈ [1, log n], so a binary search with P as an oracle gives the quantum learning algorithm (Algorithm 1), which sets N = LRn2 log n/ε2 and T = N 2nk.
quotes: Given the fact that a structured unitary set that UA(R−1) is strictly contained in UA(R) (Haferkamp et al., 2022), the boolean function P(R, ε) = BMaxS(ρun, ρˆQCA(R, A, N ), T, ε) (12) is a monotone predicate in the interval R ∈ [1, log n].
Therefore a quantum learning algorithm can be designed by a binary search program where P(R, ε) is packaged as an oracle.
Set N = LRn2 log n/ε2 and T = N 2nk
assertions.certainty_reason: An argument that rests on a cited containment result.
assertions.reader_inference: Monotonicity is true for the exact optimum. BMaxS is a randomized approximate optimizer, so the printed text does not show that P itself is monotone for every run.

assertions.value: The paper states that the subroutine BMaxS is a Bayesian optimization that takes the unknown state, the QCA state set and the LS error ε as inputs and after T steps outputs True if R ∈ UDI(ε) holds and False otherwise; Appendix I models LR(β) with a Gaussian process with prior mean zero, and the observations carry a quantum measurement error εi ∼ N(0, 1/4M) from M snapshot measurements.

assertions.value: The paper states (Theorem 2) that, given poly(n) copies of an n-qubit unknown weakly noisy state generated with depth R = O(log n) and a particular architecture A, there exists a poly(n, R, 1/ε) quantum and classical cost learning algorithm that solves the SCP(A, ε) problem; its proof is given as an outline of the sample complexity, the classical computational complexity and the iteration complexity.

assertions.reader_inference: In the proof of Lemma 6 the paper shows Tr(ρ2) ≥ Tr(ρ log ρ) and then writes the bound as n + Tr ρ2 = D2, but D2 equals n + log Tr[ρ2], not n + Tr[ρ2]. The inequality D ≤ D2 is a known property of Rényi divergences (the reader's background knowledge, not checked against a source here), so the statement is likely true although the printed proof has this slip.

assertions.value: The authors describe how a lower bound is read from the plot of min LR against the circuit depth R: draw a horizontal line at the approximation error, find the last point where the curve remains above it, and record the corresponding R; in Figure 2 (b) with ε′ = 0.25 the blue curve stays above until R = 4, giving a bound above 4L for the noisy depth 2 state, and the green curve at R = 2 gives a bound above 2L for the noisy depth 10 state.

in (b), we set ε′ = 0.25.
the blue curve remains above ε′ = 0.25 until R = 4, indicating a complexity lower bound of C0li.m12,A5 (ρTI(2, p)) > 4L

assertions.reader_inference: The threshold 0.25 is larger than 2ε = 0.02 of the setup, so a curve above 0.25 is also above the Lemma 2 threshold; the reader notes that the estimate is read by eye from a plot.

assertions.value: The authors report a stress test on the transverse-field Ising model with system sizes 1×6, 1×8 and 1×10, and state that the complexity lower bound of noisy quantum circuits does not grow linearly with circuit depth, that in all cases the weakly noisy state with depth 2 has a larger lower bound than the depth 10 state, that the variance does not increase with system size and that the gap between the two curves does not show a closing trend.
quotes: We tested the transverse-field Ising model with system sizes of 1×6, 1×8, and 1×10
Our findings indicate that the complexity lower bound of noisy quantum circuits does not grow linearly with circuit depth
In all cases, we observe that the weakly noisy state with R ̃ = 2 exhibits a larger quantum state complexity lower bound compared to the weakly noisy state with R ̃ = 10.
At the same time, the gap between the curves of quantum states with different complexities does not show a closing trend as the system size grows.
assertions.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one simulated study at three small sizes.

assertions.value: The authors state that these characteristics demonstrate the robustness of the learning algorithm against increases in system size and complexity, and that the algorithm remains reliable for predicting the complexity of largescale weakly noisy quantum states.
quotes: These characteristics demonstrate the robustness of our learning algorithm against increases in system size and complexity.
Therefore, our algorithm remains reliable for predicting the complexity of largescale weakly noisy quantum states.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim drawn from sizes of at most 10 qubits.
assertions.reader_inference: The test sizes are 6, 8 and 10 qubits (and 12 in the main text), so the claim about largescale states is an extrapolation; the paper gives no test beyond these sizes.

(2024); they also state that learning the difference between noisy ensembles and Haar-random states does not imply distinguishing pseudorandom from Haar-random ensembles.

this does not imply that the algorithm can be used to distinguish between pseudorandom ensembles and Haar-random ensembles.

assertions.value: The authors state that the algorithm needs only a quantum computer that supports quantum error mitigation, which should have 50 − 100 noisy qubits with ≥ 0.99 quantum gate fidelity, and name Eagle and Sycamore as platforms that may satisfy this; they cite Jnane et al. (2024) for error mitigation embedded in classical shadows.

As a result, our Alg 1 only require a quantum computer which supports the quantum error mitigation function, which should have 50 − 100 noisy qubits with ≥ 0.99 quantum gate fidelity.

Some popular quantum computation platforms may satisfy these requirements and can be used to prepare the required classical shadow, such as Eagle used in Ref. Kim et al. (2023) and Sycamore Arute et al. (2019).
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the mitigation result is cited.
assertions.reader_inference: Task 1 assumes an ideal quantum device, while Appendix C asks for noisy qubits with error mitigation. The reader did not find an end-to-end guarantee that joins the mitigated shadow with the bounds of Section 5.

assertions.value: The authors state, from two relative entropy inequalities with factors (1 − pg) and (1 − pl)n, that the global depolarizing channel is much weaker than local noise at the same noise strength, and that for the global depolarizing channel the algorithm can handle pg ≤ O(1) with comparable prediction accuracy.
quotes: These inequalities indicate that the global depolarizing channel is much weaker than local noise, given the same noise strength.
our algorithm is capable of handling scenarios where pg ≤ O(1), while maintaining comparable prediction accuracy.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim with no experiment for the global channel.
assertions.reader_inference: The two inequalities are upper bounds on the contraction of each channel. A smaller upper bound on one channel is not by itself a statement that the other channel contracts more, so the comparison is an inference from bounds.

assertions.value: The paper defines an architecture A, following earlier work, as a directed acyclic graph with |V| ∈ Z>0 vertices (gates) in which two edges (qubits) enter and two edges exit each vertex, and defines a circuit UA as a causal slice if there exists a qubit-reachable path between any two qubit-pairs that passes only through vertices in the architecture.
assertions.anchor: Definitions 6 and 7, Appendix E, p.17, p.17
quotes: An architecture A is a directed acyclic graph that contains |V| ∈ Z>0 vertices (gates), and two edges (qubits) enter each vertex, and two edges exit.
The circuit UA is a causal slice if there exists a qubit-reachable path between any two qubit-pairs, where the path only passes through vertices (gates) in the architecture A.
assertions.certainty_reason: Definition 6 is attributed to Haferkamp et al. and Bouland et al.

assertions.value: The authors conclude that the learning algorithm exploits the intrinsic structure of the QCA to build a learning model LR(β) whose extreme points reveal the limited-structured complexity, that the algorithm achieves optimal in terms of the circuit depth when the sample complexity of the target state is considered, and that the Bayesian optimizer is not the unique option.
quotes: The proposed quantum learning algorithm exploits the intrinsic structure of QCA to build a learning model LR(β), whose extreme points reveal the limited-structured complexity.
our algorithm achieves optimal in terms of the circuit depth
we emphasize that the Bayesian optimizer (given by Alg. 2) is not the unique option, and other optimization algorithms may also work with a similar iteration steps.
assertions.certainty_reason: Conclusions stated by the authors.
assertions.reader_inference: The body says nearly optimal (Section 5.1) and the conclusion says optimal; see the Theorem 3 entry.
